# Best deterministic Gaussian approximation of the shifted-chi-square Ring-LWE error prior

**Scope.** This compares the ideal, unwrapped noise generated by [Peikert–Regev–Stephens-Davidowitz (PRS), Definition 6.1](https://web.eecs.umich.edu/~cpeikert/pubs/rlwe-anyring.pdf) against a deterministic Gaussian. Independent embedding places draw their random widths once per batch. The result gives a sufficient statistical transfer bound for adding the same public signal and wrapping. The necessary statements are for the unwrapped noise comparison only: they do not assert a lower bound after wrapping, a new worst-case hardness reduction, or anything about a concrete scheme or its implementation.

In PRS §7 the bounded-sample spherical-error argument transfers probability of selected events after adding extra noise, conditionally on the random width vector. Our question is different: how close can the entire *marginalized* batch be made to a single Gaussian with no extra padding? [Pommeret, Distance of a Mixture from its Parent Distribution](https://doi.org/10.2307/25053463) derives orthogonal-polynomial mixture expansions; [Cai–Jeng–Jin](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2011.00781.x) analyze related heteroscedastic Gaussian mixture tests. The focus here is the exact TV profile for the stated unbounded prior and the optimum over *all* deterministic Gaussian means and covariances, not the underlying Laguerre expansion or normal local-likelihood calculation.

## 1. Prior, normalization, and statement

Let s_1 and s_2 be the numbers of real and complex places, respectively, d=s_1+s_2, and m>=1 the number of error draws using the same width vector. A real place contributes a block of k_j=m real coordinates, and a complex place contributes k_j=2m. In the latter, use the usual real orthonormal coordinates for the canonical Euclidean inner product, so the block is isotropic.

PRS use squared widths alpha^2 (f^2+W_j)/2. The independent W_j are:

    real:       W_j = chi-square(1)/(2 pi),
    complex:    W_j = chi-square(2)/(4 pi).

Indeed, the D_1 density has real variance 1/(2 pi), and each independent real part of the D_1/sqrt(2) in Definition 6.1 has half that variance. Set mu_0=1/(2 pi), epsilon=(f^2+mu_0)^(-1), Z_j=W_j-mu_0. Divide the error coordinates by their common mean standard deviation. Then the law P is a product over places whose j-th block is

    Y_j = sqrt(1+epsilon Z_j) G_j,     G_j ~ N(0,I_(k_j)),

with independent Z_j and G_j. Conditional entries in a block are independent; unconditional entries use the same scale. The mean-matched Gaussian Q is N(0,I) in these normalized coordinates. For v_j=E Z_j^2 set

    r_j=k_j/2,   K_j=r_j(r_j+1)/2=k_j(k_j+2)/8,
    a_j=epsilon^2 v_j sqrt(K_j),   T=sum_j a_j^2.

Thus the exact profile parameter is

    T = epsilon^4 [s_1 m(m+2) + s_2 m(m+1)]/(32 pi^4).      (1)

As d tends to infinity and epsilon tends to zero, for arbitrary m=m(d), if T tends to tau in [0,infinity], then

    TV(P,Q)  ->  2 Phi(sqrt(tau)/2)-1,
    inf_(all Gaussian G on the full space) TV(P,G)
             ->  2 Phi(sqrt(tau)/2)-1.                       (2)

Here Phi denotes the standard normal CDF, with endpoints 0 at tau=0 and 1 at tau=infinity. The infimum includes nonzero centers, arbitrary correlations across or within blocks, and choices depending on d or m. Degenerate Gaussians have TV one because P has a density. In particular, in this unwrapped model replacement with vanishing error is possible exactly when

    [s_1 m(m+2)+s_2 m(m+1)]/(f^2+1/(2 pi))^4 -> 0.

For T small and delta=epsilon sqrt(m) sufficiently small there is also an absolute-constant finite bound

    TV(P,Q) <= (1/2) sqrt(exp(C T)-1) + C d delta^12.         (3)

The comparison is independent of alpha since it uses an invertible common rescaling. The constants in the proof allow either signature or any mixture of the two.

## 2. Local expansion: handling unbounded widths

Let K=K_j, r=r_j, and write X=||G_j||^2/2. Under Q, X has the gamma law of shape r and unit scale. For a deterministic relative variance s>-1 its likelihood is

    R_s(X)=(1+s)^(-r) exp(X s/(1+s)).

For s,t small and positive variances the exact inner product, by the gamma integral, is

    E_Q[R_s R_t] = (1-st)^(-r).                            (4)

Here (4) is used only on |s|,|t|<1; then the integral converges. More generally the integral is infinite if st>=1. Every untruncated shifted-chi-square Z_j has positive probability of epsilon Z_j>1. By the nonnegative pairwise likelihood integral, the *untruncated* single-block chi-squared divergence to Q is therefore infinite at every epsilon>0. One cannot tensorize the uncapped L2 norm.

Define the centered, orthogonal unit-second-moment polynomials

    U=(X-r)/sqrt(r),
    H=[X^2/2-(r+1) X + K]/sqrt(K).                          (5)

They are respectively second and fourth Gaussian chaos as functions of G_j; for example, H is the degree-four Wick polynomial of the squared block norm. Their orthogonality and unit norm follow from E X^b=(r)_b. Under R_s they have exact expectations sqrt(r) s and sqrt(K) s^2. Moreover H>=-C uniformly for r>=1/2, by completing the square in (5), and all its fixed moments are uniformly bounded (e.g. Gaussian polynomial hypercontractivity). The same moment assertion holds for U.

When T is bounded, delta tends to zero, and T is comparable to d delta^4. Uniformly over the two possible Z laws, truncate by conditioning on Z<=M_delta for M_delta=C_0 log(1/delta). For C_0 large, the removed probability and absolute tail moments through fourth order are O(delta^12); the negative support is bounded. Product TV between P and its truncated version P' is O(d delta^12) by coupling. Each likelihood L'_j of the truncated mixture relative to its baseline block admits

    L'_j = 1+a_j H_j+e_j,   E_Q e_j=0,
    ||e_j||_(L^2(Q))^2 = O(delta^6)+o(delta^4),             (6)

uniformly in the block type. To see this without any interchange at the uncapped prior, let Z',Z'' be independent conditional truncated scales and z=epsilon^2 Z'Z''. Then |z|<=C epsilon^2 log^2(1/delta), r |z|=o(1), and (4) expands as

    E_Q(L'_j)^2
      = 1 + r epsilon^2 (E Z')^2
          + K epsilon^4 (E (Z')^2)^2 + O(delta^6).

Indeed, the absolute cubic remainder is at most
C (r+2)^3 E|z|^3 exp(C(r+3) sup|z|)=O(delta^6); the third absolute moment stays bounded. The first two orthogonal projections have exactly the coefficients sqrt(r) epsilon E Z' and sqrt(K) epsilon^2 E(Z')^2 from (5). The former is negligible, and the latter differs from a_j by o(delta^2). Pythagoras gives (6). In particular, \|L'_j-1\|_2^2<=C a_j^2 for all small delta, and tensorizing these *truncated* L2 norms gives (3).

Suppose now 0<tau<infinity. Since a_j=O(delta^2) and H_j>=-C, the probability law with block likelihood 1+a_j H_j is well defined and each block likelihood is at least 1/2 for small delta. Squared Hellinger distance between that product and P' is bounded by a constant times sum_j ||e_j||_2^2=o(1), using (6) and T comparable to d delta^4. Thus P has the same critical TV limit as this proxy. Under Q its log likelihood satisfies

    sum_j log(1+a_j H_j)
         = sum_j a_j H_j - (1/2) sum_j a_j^2 H_j^2 + o_Q(1)
         ->  N(-tau/2,tau).

Indeed, the sum of expected absolute cubic remainders is at most C (max a_j) T=o(1); uniform fourth moment gives the quadratic convergence and the triangular-array CLT. Evaluating TV as E_Q (1-exp(log likelihood))_+ yields the first assertion in (2) at finite positive tau. At tau=0 it follows from (3).

## 3. Why arbitrary Gaussian retuning cannot improve the critical limit

For a finite positive tau define weights w_j=a_j/sqrt(T), so sum w_j^2=1 and max|w_j|=O(d^(-1/2)). Use the scalar comparison

    F(y)=sum_j w_j H_j(y_j).

Under Q this tends to N(0,1). Under the actual (uncapped) P it tends to N(sqrt(tau),1). For the latter statement, coupling a block with G_j by s=epsilon Z_j gives the exact polynomial identity

    H_j(sqrt(1+s) G_j)
      = (1+s)^2 H_j(G_j)
          + sqrt(2(r_j+1)) s(1+s) U_j(G_j)
          + sqrt(K_j) s^2.                                 (7)

Hence its mean is a_j and its variance tends uniformly to one, since epsilon sqrt(m) tends to zero. Its fourth moment remains bounded by the uniform moments in (5) and those of Z_j. Independence and the weighted CLT give the assertion.

Let G_*=N(mu,Sigma) be any sequence of possible Gaussian replacements. At finite tau, P is contiguous with respect to Q: for sets of vanishing Q mass, their P mass vanishes by the uniformly bounded L2 likelihood of P' from (6) and the vanishing truncation error. If the affinity of G_* and Q tends to zero on a subsequence, there are sets of Q mass tending to one but G_* mass tending to zero (TV is at least one minus affinity). Their P mass tends to one; hence TV(P,G_*) tends to one there.

Otherwise consider a subsequence where this affinity is bounded below. Completing the square for Gaussian affinity gives

    -log Aff(G_*,Q)
       = (1/2) sum_l log((1+lambda_l)/(2 sqrt(lambda_l)))
          + (1/4) mu^T (I+Sigma)^(-1) mu,

where lambda_l are the eigenvalues of Sigma. This entails a uniform compact spectral interval in (0,infinity), and uniform bounds on ||Sigma-I||_F and ||mu||. Put A=Sigma^(1/2), E=Sigma-I; then also ||A-I||_F, ||A||_op are uniformly bounded.

Here is a dimension-uniform justification that F under any such G_* still tends to N(0,1). Write F as the contraction of a symmetric fourth-order tensor D with the standard-Gaussian Wick tensor of y. If P_j is the orthogonal projector onto block j, then

    D = sum_j [w_j/(8 sqrt(K_j))] sym(P_j tensor P_j),

where sym is the average of the three ways to pair four tensor indices. This follows directly from the coefficient of ||y_j||^4 and the Wick correction terms in (5). For the tensor D_j representing H_j alone, the Wick isometry gives ||D_j||_F^2=1/4!. Its one-index partial trace is proportional to P_j by block rotation invariance, with coefficient 1/(4! k_j). The blocks have disjoint supports. It follows that
- applying a matrix B on one mode of D gives Frobenius norm at most (max_j |w_j|/sqrt(4! k_j)) ||B||_F, and a vector contraction satisfies the same estimate;
- contracting D with a matrix B on any two modes gives norm at most C max_j |w_j| ||B||_F. Indeed, contraction of sym(P_j tensor P_j) produces [tr(P_j B) P_j+2P_j B P_j]/3 for symmetric B. Its norm is at most (k_j+2)||P_j B P_j||_F/3, and sqrt(K_j) is comparable to k_j.

Under the coupling Y=AX+mu for X~Q, expand Wick tensors using the generating function

    exp(z.Y-||z||^2/2)
      = exp((A^T z).X-||A^T z||^2/2)
          exp(z.mu + z^T E z/2).

The degree-four tensor coefficient with no mu,E contracts D against four copies of A. Its difference from the original tensor D tends to zero in Frobenius norm, by telescoping across modes with one A-I and the first estimate. Every other term has at least one contraction with mu or E; the two estimates show its Frobenius norm tends to zero. Further contractions with uniformly bounded mu,E remain small by Cauchy–Schwarz, and the remaining A factors have bounded operator norm. These are finitely many terms of degrees zero to four. The Wick isometry now gives ||F(Y)-F(X)||_2=o(1). Thus F under G_* tends to N(0,1) on this subsequence.

Comparing the event F>=sqrt(tau)/2 under P and G_* proves

    liminf TV(P,G_*) >= 2 Phi(sqrt(tau)/2)-1.

The affinity alternatives exhaust all subsequences, and Q attains this limiting upper bound. Taking a sequence of approximate minimizers proves the claimed infimum with no prior localization hypothesis.

## 4. Supercritical regime and the positive transfer

If T tends to infinity but delta tends to zero, select enough blocks to make the sum of their a_j^2 tend to an arbitrary fixed tau_0>0. This is possible because max a_j^2 tends to zero and the full sum diverges. The selected block count tends to infinity; every Gaussian marginal is still Gaussian. By data processing and the critical lower bound, the infimum on the full space has limit inferior at least the profile at tau_0, and tau_0 may then tend to infinity.

The same argument applies for unbounded m without assuming delta tends to zero: first keep only

    m' = min(m, max(1, ceil(epsilon^(-2) d^(-1/4))))

draws per place. Then epsilon sqrt(m') tends to zero. If this cap binds, the new parameter is at least an absolute constant times d^(1/2), and otherwise the original T is unchanged. This proves the infinite endpoint.

Finally, (3) gives a *positive* transfer guarantee: starting with the stated width prior or with the mean-matched Gaussian, take the same independently generated public rows and secret, add the identical signal term, and reduce the outputs modulo any fixed torus. This is a common Markov channel, so the resulting experiments differ in TV by at most (3). No inverse comparison after wrapping is claimed, and vanishing TV is not automatically negligible in a cryptographic asymptotic convention. In particular this result does not replace the conditional event-transfer lemma of PRS §7 when the regimes or required error scales differ.

## 5. Reproduction

Run the accompanying standalone Node.js verifier:

    node verify-prs-width-prior-gaussian-approximation.js

It checks exact gamma polynomial identities and variance profile constants, exact finite tensor contraction identities on toy blocks, and numerical positive-width likelihood integrals. The asymptotic statements and global Gaussian comparison follow from the analytic proof above.
